{"id": "39:42/q21", "question": "How does the verse's expression arrange and emphasize its claims?", "turns_on": "Which feature of the wording carries the emphasis: sequence, fronting, number, deixis, or particles.", "positions": [{"id": "39:42/q21/p1", "position": "It first gathers all souls under God's taking, then separates the retained and released kinds.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭībī calls this jamʿ wa-tafrīq; Ibn ʿĀshūr calls the fāʾ in 'so He retains' explicative of an inference from taking."}, {"id": "39:42/q21/p2", "position": "Fronting 'Allah' emphasizes or restricts the true taking to Him.", "reasons": "Ālūsī favors exclusivity from context; Ṭabāṭabāʾī connects it to angels as intermediate causes. Biqāʿī says the named subject fits the claim that only God guards people."}, {"id": "39:42/q21/p3", "position": "The plural 'souls' treats many as though one, while keeping literal plurality clear.", "reasons": "Biqāʿī calls it a plural of paucity used for many. Al-Burhān separately observes that plurals can cover few or many and cites the generic article in al-ghurufāt at 38:24."}, {"id": "39:42/q21/p4", "position": "The distal 'that,' indefinite plural 'signs,' and emphatic conclusion elevate and multiply the evidence.", "reasons": "Ālūsī gives recency, starting point and exalted rank as reasons for the demonstrative's form, and abundance and greatness for nunation. Ibn ʿĀshūr says 'indeed' presses a neglected implication."}]}
{"id": "39:42/q22", "question": "What signs does reflection on this verse reveal?", "turns_on": "Whether the primary lesson is divine uniqueness, resurrection, or conduct flowing from both.", "positions": [{"id": "39:42/q22/p1", "position": "God's exact control over death, sleep, retention and return proves His unique power, knowledge, wisdom and right to worship.", "reasons": "Al-Baghawī notes that God never errs in holding or returning. Rāzī points to ordered soul-body relations; Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Ṭabrisī infer oneness against idols. Bayḍāwī and Bursevī add mercy and the soul's persistence and fate. Ibn ʿĀshūr says tafakkur is repeated, effortful thought, and the signs are two distinct acts of divine craftsmanship encountered daily."}, {"id": "39:42/q22/p2", "position": "The daily restoration from sleep is evidence that God can resurrect the dead.", "reasons": "Muqātil and Ibn al-Jawzī make resurrection the reflective point. Biqāʿī reasons that the agent ending sleep's minor death can end greater death; al-Kawāshī and al-Kāshifī invoke death as sleep and resurrection as waking, also mentioning the Torah. Iṣlāḥī says the daily cycle rehearses renewed life."}, {"id": "39:42/q22/p3", "position": "The signs teach reliance on God and make the universe an educator in truths needed for salvation.", "reasons": "Iṣlāḥī draws exclusive trust from exclusive divine control and calls creation a lesson in Qur'anic truths; Biqāʿī says recognition eases affliction and consoles the Prophet."}]}
{"id": "39:42/q23", "question": "What does the verse imply about the soul after bodily death?", "turns_on": "How retention after death relates to survival, consciousness, and punishment before resurrection.", "positions": [{"id": "39:42/q23/p1", "position": "The soul survives separately from the body and is held for resurrection and reckoning.", "reasons": "Ṭabāṭabāʾī infers distinct existence from separation. Al-Qurṭubī describes a subtle body capable of being drawn out, wrapped, carried, seeing and smelling; 56:83 depicts its exit at the throat. Bursevī says the human spirit is questioned and rewarded or punished in the grave; Elmalılı says death is detention, cites 36:52 and 40:11, and favors ʿAlī's couplet that the dead will be questioned. His contrast with al-Kashshāf addresses whether separated disbelievers escape punishment."}, {"id": "39:42/q23/p2", "position": "The rational soul is not itself subject to death.", "reasons": "Elmalılı reports al-Kashshāf's answer to the problem of punishment after sleep-like separation."}, {"id": "39:42/q23/p3", "position": "Souls are created and dependent on God; their consciousness can be withdrawn without destroying them.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī calls the subtle soul beginningful but not perishing. Elmalılı cites 8:24 for divine control over a self's consciousness."}]}
{"id": "39:42/q24", "question": "How does this verse connect with its surrounding passage and other verses?", "turns_on": "Which neighboring claim the verse is read as developing: guardianship, divine sufficiency, guidance, or the sūra's broader death theme.", "positions": [{"id": "39:42/q24/p1", "position": "It follows 'you are not their guardian': God alone guards, takes, restores, and governs people.", "reasons": "Jishumī, Ṭabrisī, Biqāʿī and Elmalılı link 39:41 to God's continuous guardianship; Elmalılı notes 39:62. Biqāʿī says an absent, sleeping or dead deputy cannot preserve guidance."}, {"id": "39:42/q24/p2", "position": "It elaborates God's sufficiency and the Creator's sole claim to worship against powerless idols.", "reasons": "Abū Muslim connects 39:36 to God's sufficiency for the Prophet; another Jishumī report links 39:38 to the Creator's ownership of life and death. Biqāʿī says the next rejection of intercessors follows from exclusive divine power."}, {"id": "39:42/q24/p3", "position": "Death and sleep illustrate guidance and misguidance in the preceding discussion.", "reasons": "Biqāʿī pairs guidance with life and waking; Elmalılı and Rāzī as reported by Asad make the comparison, with temporary straying like sleep. Elmalılı also ties 39:30–31 and 10:108 to each person's own guidance or error. Kur'an Yolu says the argument turns from human choice in 39:41 to divine governance and then 39:43."}, {"id": "39:42/q24/p4", "position": "The passage joins other Qur'anic death and life texts.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr contrasts the order of 6:60–61; al-Sāmarrāʾī links the sūra's 'struck down' with death and sleep; Study Quran notes that 39:53 later opens mercy even to squandered souls. Iṣlāḥī says the next discussion puts life and death under God's authority."}]}
{"id": "39:42/q25", "question": "What further spiritual lessons are drawn from death and sleep?", "turns_on": "Which aspect of the soul's separation yields the lesson: remembrance, bodily instrument, unseen travel, or divine encounter.", "positions": [{"id": "39:42/q25/p1", "position": "The knower makes natural life and spirit live by remembrance and striving.", "reasons": "Sahl says dense nature lives on food, drink and pleasure, while spirit lives by remembrance; he cites the living dead of 3:169."}, {"id": "39:42/q25/p2", "position": "The body is a temporary instrument for the soul's knowledge; death can relieve its burden after spiritual harvest.", "reasons": "Bursevī cites a Mathnawī couplet, compares the body to a hunter's net, and explains the Prophet's 'death is a believer's gift'; if it fails before the harvest, 23:99–100 describes regret. A Persian line calls death a door all pass."}, {"id": "39:42/q25/p3", "position": "Sleep and spiritual shedding let the spirit visit unseen realms; wakeful shedding can bring stronger witnessing.", "reasons": "Bursevī says subtle spirits can travel beyond dense bodies, renew witnessing and longing. He explains sleep's pleasure as merciful care and death's pain as the Angel's hand. He identifies brain vapors and relaxed nerves as sleep's bodily process."}, {"id": "39:42/q25/p4", "position": "The believer's death is a divine meeting for which God prepares the soul.", "reasons": "Bursevī cites a sacred report of divine hesitation over taking a believer: he denies perplexity and reads it as showing prepared blessings until the servant longs for death. Sharḥ al-Sunna instead says God repeatedly sends harms but delays their fatal effect; dislike of death concerns its severity. A report says none sees God before death, and Persian verse speaks of dying before death for vision and security."}]}
{"id": "39:42/q26", "question": "What other claims are attached to this discussion?", "turns_on": "These are distinct accompanying claims rather than competing explanations of one phrase.", "positions": [{"id": "39:42/q26/p1", "position": "Life and death are alternating accidents that only God can produce.", "reasons": "Jishumī reports this kalām account."}, {"id": "39:42/q26/p2", "position": "Life is an accident, and a loss of necessary knowledge can occur while life and spirit remain; death's seizure excludes life.", "reasons": "Jishumī reports this distinct analysis."}, {"id": "39:42/q26/p3", "position": "Guidance and misguidance are human acts, while God intended the revealed book to guide and to command action.", "reasons": "Jishumī also says religious argumentation is valid and worship belongs to the Creator of blessings rather than one unable to benefit or harm."}, {"id": "39:42/q26/p4", "position": "Traditional formulaic accounts of rhetorical inimitability fail to convince modern Arabic readers.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shāṭiʾ criticizes rigid templates and inflated language, including al-Khaṭṭābī's account."}]}
{"id": "39:53/q01", "question": "How does this verse turn from the surrounding warnings to its invitation?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "39:53/q01/p1", "position": "After warnings of death, loss, and punishment, God turns through the Prophet to a tender invitation that restores hope while retaining the call to repent and submit.", "reasons": "Biqaʿi says prolonged threats risk alienation; Abu Hayyan says the preceding threat and possible ransom prepare hope and fear; Ibn ʿAshur calls the vocative a fresh opening; al-Tabatabaʾi reads seven connected verses calling to Islam, submission and righteous action; Study Quran points to the desperate death passage; Islahi says the section opposes reliance on idols and intercessors and urges turning before regret."}]}

{"id": "39:53/q03", "question": "Who are the servants addressed by يَٰعِبَادِىَ?", "turns_on": "Whether the possessive ʿibād conventionally confines the address to believers, and whether the following verses show an initial call to polytheists or allow a universal address.", "positions": [{"id": "39:53/q03/p1", "position": "The address extends to every sinner, believer or polytheist; reported occasions do not limit its general wording.", "reasons": "Tabari expressly prefers the general wording over particular occasions; Ibn ʿAtiyya extends it to Resurrection; Razi, Baydawi and Bursevi distinguish general text from particular occasion. Bursevi cites 17:5 against a believers-only rule. Tabatabaʾi points to the following denial and arrogance at 39:59; Study Quran says all humanity. Al-Qurazi says all people. The Prophet is reported to have said the Wahshi promise applies generally; Tabatabaʾi regards application to the Imams' Shiʿa as an instance, not a restriction."}, {"id": "39:53/q03/p2", "position": "The first addressees are polytheists, especially Meccans with pre-Islamic sins.", "reasons": "Zayd b. Aslam and Ibn ʿAbbas specify Meccan idolaters; Ibn ʿAshur invokes the next call to submit and later references to denial and arrogance (39:54, 56, 59), and judges other occasion reports weak or unknown. Tabatabaʾi finds the polytheist reading more plausible than believer-only; al-Burhan says the gentle call encourages embracing Islam."}, {"id": "39:53/q03/p3", "position": "The possessive address refers to sinful believers.", "reasons": "Baydawi, Burhan and reported views in Bursevi, Alusi and Tabatabaʾi invoke Qurʾanic use of God's possessive ʿibād, including 76:6. Razi says the address answers believers' prayer at 3:193 and 40:60, whereas unbelievers did not pray; Tabari says obligations also address believers. Reports connect it to persecuted Muslims and to people who thought major sinners damned."}]}
{"id": "39:53/q04", "question": "What does calling sinners 'My servants' accomplish?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "39:53/q04/p1", "position": "The intimate possessive and direct call honor sinners, invite them toward God, and awaken hope and compassion.", "reasons": "Razi says servanthood evokes need and poverty and possession reassures; Baydawi and Abu Hayyan connect it to self-inflicted harm; Samīn notes direct attention and honor; Biqaʿi calls it the sweetness of belonging. Qushayri says it lifts sinners' heads and lowers the self-assured obedient. Kashf al-Asrar contrasts human love with angelic servitude and says God veils particular faults. Ibn ʿAshur says it prepares acceptance; Suyuti calls the mode tender; Tabatabaʾi recalls lordship and the duty of obedience. Burhan gives an inward progression from Islam and obedience to excellence, comparing 29:56."}]}
{"id": "39:53/q05", "question": "What can عِبَاد mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "39:53/q05/p1", "position": "It denotes servants or slaves, including God's servants and household slaves.", "reasons": "Damghani compares 43:15 and 24:32; Junayd defines true servanthood as turning from distractions to worship."}]}
{"id": "39:53/q06", "question": "What does أَسْرَفُوا۟ mean here?", "turns_on": "Whether the term is explained by its general sense of exceeding limits or specified by the serious sins at issue.", "positions": [{"id": "39:53/q06/p1", "position": "It means crossing the proper limit in any action, here excessive sin and wrongdoing.", "reasons": "Al-Raghib, cited by Bursevi and Tabatabaʾi, says excessive spending is the common use but the root applies to any action; Alusi approves that breadth while reporting a two-step figurative derivation from spending; Elmalili and Damghani agree. Biqaʿi says transgressors put things out of place and burden themselves. Tabatabaʾi includes shirk and major and minor sins; Study Quran notes pre-Islamic killing and cites 3:154, 5:50, 33:33, 48:26 and 10:12."}, {"id": "39:53/q06/p2", "position": "It especially denotes grave sins and indecencies.", "reasons": "Muqatil names shirk, murder and adultery, calling shirk the greatest excess; Mujahid specifies pre-Islamic killing. Mawrdi separately allows sins while retaining faith. Thalabi, Wahidi, Ibn al-Jawzi, Ibn ʿUmar and Bursevi name major sins or shameful acts."}]}
{"id": "39:53/q07", "question": "How does عَلَىٰٓ أَنفُسِهِمْ work grammatically?", "turns_on": "Which implied verbal sense governs ʿalā: doing injury or bearing a burden.", "positions": [{"id": "39:53/q07/p1", "position": "The preposition ʿalā supplies the sense of committing an offense against oneself.", "reasons": "Bursevi, Alusi and Elmalili explain the verb's construction by an incorporated sense of injury; Alusi says this need not be literal and also reports the alternative sense of bearing a burden."}, {"id": "39:53/q07/p2", "position": "The construction can evoke bearing a burden upon oneself.", "reasons": "Alusi reports this as another explanation of the preposition."}]}
{"id": "39:53/q08", "question": "Why say that sinners transgressed against themselves?", "turns_on": "Whether the self-directed wording only evokes compassion or also limits the promise where another person's right is involved.", "positions": [{"id": "39:53/q08/p1", "position": "Their sins injure and burden their own souls, a reminder that invites divine compassion.", "reasons": "Razi and Alusi argue self-inflicted harm is already sufficient injury; Baydawi links the wording to compassion; Abu Hayyan and Kuran Yolu say sin first soils the sinner; Biqaʿi describes removal from divine presence. Qushayri hears renewed hope even for a repeated returner."}, {"id": "39:53/q08/p2", "position": "Wrongs against other people require discharge of the injured person's claim before forgiveness.", "reasons": "Biqaʿi infers this from the wording's restriction to transgression against oneself."}]}
{"id": "39:53/q09", "question": "How is the nūn of تَقْنَطُوا۟ read?", "turns_on": "The transmitted stem vowel and dialect pattern of qaniṭa; the prohibition's sense remains the same.", "positions": [{"id": "39:53/q09/p1", "position": "It is read with fatḥa: taqnaṭū.", "reasons": "Thalabi says the other readers use it; Jishumi, Ibn ʿAtiyya and Razi call it the majority reading and a dialect form. Qurtubi compares 15:56."}, {"id": "39:53/q09/p2", "position": "It is read with kasra: taqniṭū.", "reasons": "Thalabi names Abu ʿAmr, al-Aʿmash, Yahya b. Waththab, ʿIsa, al-Kisaʾi and Yaʿqub; Jishumi names Abu ʿAmr, al-Kisaʾi and Yaʿqub; Ibn ʿAtiyya names Abu ʿAmr and Ibn Waththab; Nasafi names ʿAli and Basrans. Elmalili says hope urges immediate repentance rather than more sin; the report about a despairing believer is reflected in prophetic warnings."}, {"id": "39:53/q11/p2", "position": "Despair and distrust of mercy can lead people to seek idols or alleged i

{"id": "39:53/q12", "question": "What is the mercy of God from which they must not despair?", "turns_on": "Whether forgiveness is contained in mercy or supplied through a strained implied parallel clause.", "positions": [{"id": "39:53/q12/p1", "position": "It includes forgiveness first, then God's further beneficence and favor.", "reasons": "Baydawi and Bursevi place forgiveness before further favor; Bursevi says forgiveness shields from punishment and mercy then gives. Bursevi cites the hundred portions of mercy report, including the mare sparing her foal and ninety-nine portions retained by God; a report of God rescuing a man who invoked Him as Compassionate illustrates its reach."}, {"id": "39:53/q12/p2", "position": "A proposed ellipsis coordinates mercy and forgiveness in both the ban and the reason for it.", "reasons": "Alusi reports a proposed omitted-symmetry analysis, 'do not despair of mercy and forgiveness, for God forgives and shows mercy,' but considers it strained."}]}
{"id": "39:53/q13", "question": "Why say رَّحْمَةِ ٱللَّهِ rather than 'My mercy'?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "39:53/q13/p1", "position": "The shift to God's name magnifies the scope and grounds of mercy.", "reasons": "Razi, Abu Hayyan, Biqaʿi and Alusi invoke the supreme name and its encompassing attributes; Samīn notes the shift from first to third person and the explicit name. {"id": "39:53/q14", "question": "What does forgiveness mean in the promise?", "turns_on": "Whether the note explains the act of pardon itself or its possible timing.", "positions": [{"id": "39:53/q14/p1", "position": "It is overlooking sin and its punishment, either concealing it or erasing it from the record.", "reasons": "Alusi reports both analyses. Biqaʿi says God can erase sins and traces without blame or punishment and then honor the forgiven; Bursevi distinguishes pardon that erases sin, citing 11:114, from forgiveness that can turn bad deeds into good, citing 25:70. Gabriel tells Abraham a forgiven sin can become a good deed."}, {"id": "39:53/q14/p2", "position": "Forgiveness can occur at once or after punishment and remains God's choice.", "reasons": "Razi says sinners cannot know that punishment is entirely removed; Baydawi says pardon can follow delay; Bursevi says even innumerable sins may be forgiven by pardon or after punishment, as God wills."}]}
{"id": "39:53/q15", "question": "Which sins and sinners can receive the forgiveness promised here?", "turns_on": "Whether repentance is required or merely one route to forgiveness, how 4:48/4:116 qualifies this verse, and whether pardon of the penitent is certain.", "positions": [{"id": "39:53/q15/p1", "position": "All sins, including shirk, are forgiven when their doer repents and turns to God; unrepented shirk remains excluded.", "reasons": "Muqatil cites 25:68–70; Tabari cites 4:48 and 19:60 and allows other sins by will. Zamakhshari treats the Qur'an as one coherent discourse whose stated repentance condition governs unstated cases; Abu Hayyan identifies and disputes this Muʿtazilite restriction. Ibn Kathir cites 9:104, 4:110, 4:145–46, 5:73–74 and 85:10, and says dying in shirk rules out an unconditioned reading; Qurtubi cites 20:82. Tabatabaʾi reads the seven verses together, rejects intercession here because it excludes shirk, and distinguishes 4:48 as a different case. Asad cites 6:54 and 4:110; Study Quran cites 4:48 and 4:116. Thawban's inclusive answer is reported repeatedly, although Ahmad 22362 and Tabatabaʾi 39:53–61 transmit the opposite answer."}, {"id": "39:53/q15/p2", "position": "Apart from unrepented shirk, God may forgive even unrepentant sins at His discretion.", "reasons": "Baydawi and Alusi say restricting the apparent promise to repentance narrows its wording; 4:48 reserves lesser sins to God's will. Tabari distinguishes grace and just requital; Ibn ʿAtiyya calls the restriction consensus; Bursevi cites concealed sins forgiven on Judgment Day, reads 4:17 as excluding last-gasp repentance and says idolatry without repentance violates wisdom. Alusi gives seventeen textual indications: servant address and possession, self-harm, unlimited ban on despair, divine name and its repetition, causal inna, definite sins and all, final cause, intensive and objectless ghafur, exclusivity and mercy after forgiveness. Kuran Yolu makes 'if He wills' explicit in translation and warns against an unrestricted guarantee for every person."}, {"id": "39:53/q15/p3", "position": "All sins are forgiven through repentance alone; an unrepentant grave sinner receives no such pardon.", "reasons": "Zamakhshari and the Muʿtazilites argue that the Qur'an is a coherent discourse, so repentance conditions stated elsewhere qualify this verse; Alusi says they deny forgiveness of grave sins without repentance and see no possibility of abrogation. Abu Hayyan identifies this as their disputed doctrine."}, {"id": "39:53/q15/p4", "position": "The promise concerns minor sins when major sins are avoided, or repentants and people with minor but no major sins.", "reasons": "Mawrdi reports forgiveness of minor sins upon avoiding major ones; Nahhas and Qurtubi identify repentants or minor sinners, citing the next command in 39:54. Tabatabaʾi reports a different restriction to minor sins after excluding threatened major sins and shirk."}, {"id": "39:53/q15/p5", "position": "Every sin is eligible for cause-free forgiveness except shirk.", "reasons": "Tabatabaʾi reports this inference from 4:116, but argues forgiveness has causes such as repentance or intercession and that this context requires repentance. Kuran Yolu rejects a guaranteed pardon irrespective of faith or turning as encouraging moral laxity."}, {"id": "39:53/q15/p6", "position": "God's pardon is guaranteed to the penitent.", "reasons": "One Sunni group in Ibn ʿAtiyya reads the apparent Qur'anic promise as certain; Qurtubi cites 20:82. A different reported group leaves even the penitent subject to divine will, albeit with predominant hope."}, {"id": "39:53/q15/p7", "position": "Even a penitent's forgiveness remains subject to God's will, though hope predominates.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAtiyya reports this alternative and contrasts fear for the unrepentant sinner."}]}
{"id": "39:53/q16", "question": "How is جَمِيعًا construed?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "39:53/q16/p1", "position": "It is accusative as a circumstantial expression.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAtiyya gives the iʿrāb."}]}
{"id": "39:53/q17", "question": "Why add جَمِيعًا to 'the sins'?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "39:53/q17/p1", "position": "The definite noun and 'all' emphasize comprehensive forgiveness, however many or grave the sins.", "reasons": "Razi, Baydawi, Biqaʿi and Bursevi stress the reinforced totality; Bursevi notes the definite article; Ibn ʿAshur says the closing divine names remove the objection from sheer number. Alusi reads the definite noun and all as evidence for including unrepented sins; al-Akhfash, cited by Zarkashi, allows an affirmative extra min in another wording to preserve the same 'all sins' sense."}]}
{"id": "39:53/q18", "question": "What variant additions to the forgiveness clause are reported?", "turns_on": "The wording and attribution of supplementary recitations, and whether they function as explanatory glosses.", "positions": [{"id": "39:53/q18/p1", "position": "A reading adds 'for whom He wills' (لمن يشاء).", "reasons": "Farra attributes it to Ibn ʿAbbas in ʿAbd Allah's codex; Tabari, Nahhas, Thalabi, Ibn ʿAtiyya, Tabrisi and Qurtubi associate it with Ibn Masʿud/ʿAbd Allah; Razi and Kashshaf also name Ibn ʿAbbas. Nahhas calls it an explanatory gloss; Zamakhshari interprets the will as the will to forgive penitents under wisdom and justice."}, {"id": "39:53/q18/p2", "position": "A Prophetic recitation is reported with 'and He does not care' (ولا يبالي).", "reasons": "Asma bint Yazid transmits the addition in Ahmad, Thalabi, Baghawi, Ibn Kathir and Tirmidhi; Tirmidhi calls it hasan gharib, knows only the Thabit–Shahr route and identifies Asma as Umm Salama al-Ansariyya. Kashshaf attributes a reading also to Fatima; Nasafi compares the denial of concern to 91:15; Nahhas treats variants as explanatory glosses. Qurtubi and Durr transmit Asma's recitation in forms without an explicit addition, so reports differ in wording."}]}
{"id": "39:53/q19", "question": "What do ٱلْغَفُورُ and ٱلرَّحِيمُ each convey?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "39:53/q19/p1", "position": "The Forgiving removes sins and grounds for punishment; the Merciful gives favor, virtues, or reward after forgiveness.", "reasons": "Razi, Bursevi and Nasafi distinguish removal of punishment or grief from bestowal of mercy and reward; Qashani reads removal of excess and deficiency and then virtues. Baydawi notes mercy after forgiveness. Samarraʾi says the faʿūl pattern makes ghafūr wholly characterized by forgiveness, compares the material consumed in its use, notes its gender and plural behavior, and distinguishes it from faʿʿāl."}]}
{"id": "39:53/q20", "question": "How does the final clause strengthen the assurance?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "39:53/q20/p1", "position": "Inna, the pronoun huwa, repeated divine name and intensive attributes emphasize that God is supremely forgiving and merciful.", "reasons": "

{"id": "39:53/q21", "question": "What occasion of revelation is reported for this verse?", "turns_on": "Different reported audiences and timelines: pagan questioners, Wahshi, coerced apostates, or Muslims judging major sinners; some authors invoke the Meccan date and general wording.", "positions": [{"id": "39:53/q21/p1", "position": "Meccan polytheists with past idolatry, murders and sexual sins asked whether conversion, migration or expiation could still avail them.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbas gives several forms: they challenged a claim that idol worship and unlawful killing were unforgivable, or came to the Prophet after many murders and fornications; Bukhari and Muslim transmit the latter, linking 25:68 and 39:53. Qatada and al-Suddi report similar fears; Ibn Zayd extends the revelation through 39:58. Al-Suyuti calls one Ibn ʿAbbas chain sound. Al-Wasit adds fighting and hostility toward the Prophet. This is the initial target favored by Ibn ʿAshur, who regards other occasions as weak or unknown."}, {"id": "39:53/q21/p2", "position": "Wahshi, killer of Hamza, sought assurance that he could repent or convert despite shirk, murder and adultery.", "reasons": "Accounts differ in sequence: Muqatil says Wahshi converted after 25:68 and 25:70 and Meccans then sought their own assurance; others place 39:53 after questions about 25:68–70, 19:60, 4:48 or 4:116. Abu Saʿid places this verse after Wahshi and companions had converted and feared 25:68. A detailed account has Wahshi fleeing, receiving a messenger's list of faith, renunciation, purification and prayer, then accepting Islam as Abu Harb. Another says the Prophet asked how Hamza died, told Wahshi to hide his face, and Wahshi died in Syria; al-Kalbi's version adds later drinking, whose location/wording Tabatabaʾi questions. Tabrisi, Tabatabaʾi and Ibn ʿAshur challenge the chronology or reliability because a Meccan passage precedes Wahshi's post-Hijra conversion; Tabrisi allows the verse later being recited to him. Tabatabaʾi calls the extended exchange fabricated; others report no grading."}, {"id": "39:53/q21/p3", "position": "Muslims coerced into apostasy during attempted migration feared that repentance could not be accepted; Umar sent them the passage.", "reasons": "Reports name Hisham b. al-ʿAs, ʿAyyash b. Abi Rabiʿa, al-Walid b. al-Walid and others. Umar, ʿAyyash and Hisham arranged to migrate; Hisham was detained, and Abu Jahl and al-Harith tricked ʿAyyash with a story about his mother. Umar wrote the revelation to Hisham and others; Hisham repeatedly read it in Dhu Tuwa, prayed for understanding, then rejoined the Prophet in Medina, later dying at Ajnadayn. Some reports say the verse descended after the Prophet reached Medina, whereas Ibn ʿAshur says Umar merely heard an earlier Meccan revelation then. Ibn ʿAtiyya attributes the account also to Qatada, al-Suddi and Ibn Abi Ishaq."}, {"id": "39:53/q21/p4", "position": "The verse also corrects Muslims who thought every major sinner was Hell-bound or that major sin erased good deeds.", "reasons": "A reported group says God can forgive whom He wills. Ibn ʿUmar says companions feared 47:33 invalidated deeds, then 4:48 ended blanket condemnation; thereafter they feared for sinners and hoped for others. A separate view concerns Muslims excessive in worship who feared their earlier pre-Islamic sins."}]}
{"id": "39:53/q22", "question": "Where and how much of this passage is said to have been revealed in Medina?", "turns_on": "How to reconcile a Meccan sūra with reports involving Wahshi and Medina-era coerced converts, and how many verses an exception covers.", "positions": [{"id": "39:53/q22/p1", "position": "Verse 53 is a Medinan exception to the Meccan sūra.", "reasons": "Baghawi and Zarkashi classify this verse alone as the exception; Study Quran reports a view restricting the Wahshi passage to 53."}, {"id": "39:53/q22/p2", "position": "Three verses beginning at 53 are Medinan, associated with Wahshi.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAtiyya reports three excepted verses, and Tabari's ʿAtaʾ report places them in Medina; Suyuti's Itqan lists the same exception. Study Quran says many commentators take 53–55 as Medinan."}, {"id": "39:53/q22/p3", "position": "Seven verses, or the passage from 53 to the end, are Medinan; another report assigns 53–59 to Wahshi.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAtiyya records the seven-verse and through-the-end variants; Study Quran records 53–59 as the Wahshi passage."}, {"id": "39:53/q22/p4", "position": "The passage was revealed in Mecca; Umar encountered or used it later in Medina.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAshur explains Umar's phrase 'God revealed it' as hearing after emigration and notes Umar was occupied preparing to migrate; Tabrisi and Tabatabaʾi reject a post-Hijra Wahshi occasion on this chronology."}]}
{"id": "39:53/q23", "question": "How does this verse relate to other verses about sin, repentance and mercy?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "39:53/q23/p1", "position": "It extends the Qur'anic call to repent and seek forgiveness and is read alongside both inclusive promises and the shirk exception.", "reasons": "Tabari cites believers' confession in 3:147; Ibn Kathir cites 9:104, 4:110, 4:145–46, 5:73–74 and 85:10; Asad and Study Quran cite 4:110. Muqatil and occasion reports link 25:68–70. Tabatabaʾi treats the next calls to turn and submit as the cause of forgiveness and argues 4:48 addresses a different case; Kuran Yolu also appeals to 39:54, whereas Baydawi and Alusi take 4:48 as permitting pardon of lesser sins by will. Qurtubi notes 13:6 as a counterexample raised against Ibn ʿUmar's most-hopeful claim. Asad points to an earlier note on 39:10 without giving its contents."}]}
{"id": "39:53/q24", "question": "Why is this verse singled out as a source of hope?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "39:53/q24/p1", "position": "Many authorities call it the Qur'an's broadest or most hopeful promise; the Prophet is reported to prize it above the world.", "reasons": "Ibn Masʿud, ʿAli, Ibn ʿUmar, ʿAbd Allah b. ʿAmr and others give the superlative; Ibn Masʿud also ranks 2:255, 16:90 and 65:2–3 in other categories. Thawban repeatedly reports the Prophet valuing it above the world. Study Quran and Itqan list other candidates including 4:48, 4:116, 24:22, 33:47, 42:19, 42:22 and 93:5; a report from ʿAli also calls 93:5 more hopeful, and Ibn ʿAbbas counters Ibn ʿUmar with 11:114. Tustari calls it the clearest compassion because God remembers servants first; Yahya b. Muʿadh calls it a treasure for believers. Samarraʾi links ghafur's intensive form to its reputation."}]}
{"id": "39:53/q25", "question": "What reports illustrate the extent and availability of repentance?", "turns_on": "The reports illustrate distinct cases and differ about the time, grounds, and reach of pardon.", "positions": [{"id": "39:53/q25/p1", "position": "Repentance remains open until the soul's final departure, with divine help and generous accounting.", "reasons": "Tustari and Sulami's Sahl say even a return at the last breath is received, while Bursevi says before the final breath or death rattle. A report in Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Kathir and Durr describes Satan's request for power, Adam's plea, a protective guardian for each child, good deeds multiplied tenfold or more, single or erased bad deeds, and repentance while the soul remains in the body; it ends with this verse. The accounts vary on the exact final moment."}, {"id": "39:53/q25/p2", "position": "A killer of one hundred was accepted after setting out toward a town of worshipers.", "reasons": "The Sahihayn report, cited by Ibn Kathir, has a monk deny hope after ninety-nine murders; the killer makes it one hundred, then a learned man advises migration. Mercy and punishment angels dispute him; measurement finds him a span nearer the good town, and his dying movement and God's shifting of the towns favor mercy. Baghawi's excerpt only begins the report at nine killings."}, {"id": "39:53/q25/p3", "position": "Prophetic reports say vast sins can be forgiven after faith, regret or seeking forgiveness, and God would bring repentant sinners if people did not sin.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathir reports an old man forgiven after confessing betrayal and affirming monotheism, a prayer for abundant forgiveness linked to 53:32, regret as atonement, and God's love of a repeated penitent; he notes the latter route is absent from canonical compilers. Anas says sins filling heaven and earth can be forgiven after seeking forgiveness. Abu Ayyub transmitted the replacement-sinners saying through Ahmad, Muslim and Tirmidhi; Ibn Kathir gives further routes. Study Quran repeats it. The Prophet also urged Aisha to repent if she had committed the alleged wrong, saying God accepts repentance."}, {"id": "39:53/q25/p4", "position": "A grave sinner was forgiven after the Prophet prayed, though the reported limit mentions shirk and murder.", "reasons": "Thalabi relates al-Zuhri's report of a youth who confessed grave robbery and intercourse with a corpse. The source gives no grading."}, {"id": "39:53/q25/p5", "position": "God calls even those who utter extreme claims about Him, including Pharaoh, to repent.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbas names claims about Jesus, Ezra, divine poverty or restraint and Trinity (5:74), then Pharaoh's self-deification (79:24; 28:38), and says barring repentance after this denies God's Book."}, {"id": "39:53/q25/p6", "position": "A murderer or one w

ho helps murder may face an especially severe warning.", "reasons": "Ibn Majah reports the Prophet's warning that even assisting a believer's murder by half a word brings a person before God marked as despairing of His mercy."}, {"id": "39:53/q25/p7", "position": "Knowledge and invocation of God's mercy can lead to rescue even when no good deed is found.", "reasons": "Durr reports Gabriel's question about a person among Hell's people with no useful good deed, followed by a rescue report for one who invoked God as the Compassionate, the Bestower; a report to David says relieving distress is good and that one who knows God should not despair."}]}
{"id": "39:53/q26", "question": "What inward reading is given to despair and the promise?", "turns_on": "Whether the emphasis falls on remaining spiritual light, the special community, or prior divine care.", "positions": [{"id": "39:53/q26/p1", "position": "Despair reflects lost spiritual receptivity and veiling; retained light of divine unity leaves hope and makes forgiveness possible.", "reasons": "Qashani says total veiling by created material nature severs the bond with God; a trace of primordial light can still recognize mercy. Bursevi says mercy precedes wrath, contrasts qunūṭ with total despair and connects the light of unity to 4:48. Qashani says the address itself signals the servant's relation to God."}, {"id": "39:53/q26/p2", "position": "The promise belongs in a special way to monotheists of Muhammad's community.", "reasons": "Qashani reports a comparison with Noah's people being promised forgiveness of some sins at 71:4; Tustari refuses to disavow sinful members of this community, including killers, adulterers and thieves. Yahya b. Muʿadh calls the verse a treasure guaranteeing pardon to believers."}, {"id": "39:53/q26/p3", "position": "Servanthood counsels dependence on prior divine care rather than confidence in deeds or despair over shortcomings.", "reasons": "Al-Jurayri says divine care precedes worship. {"id": "39:53/q27", "question": "How do the unattached grammatical notes bear on the verse's wording?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "39:53/q27/p1", "position": "The notes give general analyses of ellipsis, exception particles, predication, rebuke, and lamentation without stating an application to this verse.", "reasons": "Sibawayh analyzes implicit baʿḍ and adjectival versus verbal exception structures, including laysa, lā yakūn, ʿadā, khalā, mā, ḥāshā and sawāk; al-Khalil, Yunus and others differ. Another passage analyzes noun-like comparatives and ḥasbuk, nominative and genitive patterns, emphatic bāʾ, and Arab usage. A third covers accusative elliptical rebukes, a Banu Asad warning, poetry, verb replacement and nominative predicates, with ʿIsa allowing a present-state reading in Farazdaq's oath. A fourth covers the lamentation alif on adjectives, constructs and compounds: al-Khalil rejects Yunus's adjective ending. None of these notes supplies a grammatical claim about the present verse."}]}
{"id": "39:53/q28", "question": "What reports specifically ask whether forgiveness includes shirk?", "turns_on": "Whether the transmitted reply expressly includes the polytheist or the report instead points to 4:48.", "positions": [{"id": "39:53/q28/p1", "position": "The Prophet is reported to affirm repeatedly that the promise can include one who associated partners with God.", "reasons": "Thawban's report in Ibn Abi Hatim and Study Quran gives the threefold affirmative response; the question concerns the extent of the verse's hope."}, {"id": "39:53/q28/p2", "position": "After repeated questions about shirk, 4:48 was revealed to qualify this verse's promise.", "reasons": "Abu Mujlaz says the Prophet stayed silent until 4:48 descended; Tabatabaʾi reports Ibn ʿUmar saying the Prophet disliked the question and cited the verse. Durr gives another version of the question and descent."}]}
{"id": "39:53/q29", "question": "Can hope in forgiveness be turned into assurance that sin is harmless?", "turns_on": "The notes distinguish wide access to repentance from a guarantee that sin has no consequence.", "positions": [{"id": "39:53/q29/p1", "position": "No: the verse does not support the Murji'ite claim that faith makes sin harmless.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAshur explicitly rejects that inference; the promise still urges repentance."}, {"id": "39:53/q29/p2", "position": "No particular sin should be declared beyond possible forgiveness, and all servants need pardon.", "reasons": "Abu al-Jawza says he knew no Companion or scholar who named an unforgivable particular sin; al-Hasan marvels that even killers of God's allies are invited to repent; a Prophetic couplet asks full pardon since no servant is without sin."}]}
{"id": "39:53/q30", "question": "Is there one agreed original audience for the verse?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "39:53/q30/p1", "position": "Interpreters report several competing original audiences.", "reasons": "Thalabi introduces his set of reports by stating that interpreters differ about whom the address concerns."}]}
{"id": "39:55/q01", "question": "Whom does the command to follow address?", "turns_on": "Whether the address continues the earlier address to God's servants and whether following the Qur'an is chiefly a new demand on polytheists; the jinn reading departs from the apparent sense according to al-Alusi.", "positions": [{"id": "39:55/q01/p1", "position": "Both believers and unbelievers are addressed, each according to their situation.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi connects the address with the earlier 'servants' and says the Qur'an came through Muhammad for all. Ibn Ashur says polytheists must embrace monotheism and Islam, whereas sinning believers must repent and increase good works. Al-Tabataba'i says revelation was sent to both groups."}, {"id": "39:55/q01/p2", "position": "The directive is chiefly for polytheists.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur says Muslims already follow the Qur'an, as indicated by the depiction of God's servants in 39:17–18."}, {"id": "39:55/q01/p3", "position": "The addressees could be jinn.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi calls this less apparent; it takes the revealed material as the heavenly books and the Qur'an as their best."}]}
{"id": "39:55/q02", "question": "What is the 'best of what was sent down' to follow?", "turns_on": "Whether 'best' names the whole Qur'an, a kind of revealed material, a narrower class of rulings, the safest conduct, or the most transformative inward and moral guidance. Al-Tabataba'i objects that restricting it to reported subsets repeats the preceding command to submit; Ali ibn Isa contests the abrogation gloss.", "positions": [{"id": "39:55/q02/p1", "position": "The Qur'an itself is the best revealed book and is to be followed as a whole.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjaj, al-Wahidi, al-Razi, Bursevi, Islahi and Study Quran cite 39:23's 'best discourse'; al-Qurtubi and al-Baghawi say all the Qur'an is good. Ibn Zayd and al-Qurtubi contrast it with Torah, Gospel and Psalms and its authority over abrogated earlier books. Al-Biqa'i adds its best teachings. Islahi calls it final, complete, protected from alteration, suited to natural religion without earlier scriptures' harsh directives, unmatched lucid Arabic for Arabs, doubly beneficial in its mutashabih and mathani form, and familiar through Abraham's religion; these gifts warrant wholehearted acceptance. Al-Alusi gives the less apparent jinn and heavenly-books version. Most exegetes reported by Kuran Yolu identify the revealed thing as Qur'an."}, {"id": "39:55/q02/p2", "position": "Follow God's commands in revelation and avoid disobedience and prohibited acts.", "reasons": "Al-Hasan says revelation also names evil to shun and lesser or permissible things one need not desire; al-Tabari includes its commands, prohibitions, reports, parables, stories, arguments, promises and warnings. Ibn Atiyya adds clear beliefs, promises, threats and forbearance, with understanding followed by action. Study Quran says revelation achieves its purpose when its injunctions are practiced. Al-Tabataba'i's reported version includes obligatory and recommended acts, avoidance of forbidden and disliked acts, and no requirement concerning the permitted."}, {"id": "39:55/q02/p3", "position": "Follow what God commands in His Book.", "reasons": "This is al-Suddi's recurring gloss; it singles out commands without separately explaining prohibitions."}, {"id": "39:55/q02/p4", "position": "Follow the abrogating rulings rather than the abrogated ones.", "reasons": "Ibn Isa, al-Jubba'i and others give this interpretation; al-Razi cites 2:106, promising a better or equivalent replacement. Al-Alusi says the comparative allows two analyses here. Ali ibn Isa objects that an abrogated ruling can still be good, though following its replacement is better."}, {"id": "39:55/q02/p5", "position": "Follow binding or strict duties rather than dispensations.", "reasons": "Al-Mawardi proposes strict duties over dispensations; al-Baydawi calls these decisive rulings; Bursevi says binding duties; al-Alusi reports decisive obligations and says the comparative is literal in that formulation."}, {"id": "39:55/q02/p6", "position": "Choose the safest course that brings salvation, including repentance and steady obedience.", "reasons": "Al-Baydawi and those following him give this reading; Bursevi names repentance and sustained obedience. Al-Alusi says the comparative retains its ordinary force."}, {"id": "39:55/q02/p7", "position": "Follow the decisive verses and leave knowledge of ambiguous verses to God.", "reasons": "Ibn Zayd gives this distinction as reported by al-Tha'labi and al-Qurtubi."}, {"id": "39:55/q02/p8", "position": "The best is obedience in lawful and unlawful matters.", "reasons": "Muqatil frames it as the

Qur'an's teachings in these matters; Ibn Ziyad gives the same practical scope."}, {"id": "39:55/q02/p9", "position": "Follow revealed legal rulings concerning lawful and unlawful matters, excluding narratives.", "reasons": "Al-Tabataba'i reports this restricted view of revealed material."}, {"id": "39:55/q02/p10", "position": "Follow obligatory and supererogatory obedience, excluding merely permissible acts.", "reasons": "This is a view reported by al-Tabrisi; al-Tabataba'i reports a close formulation that also distinguishes forbidden and disliked acts."}, {"id": "39:55/q02/p11", "position": "Fulfill the obligations.", "reasons": "Zayd ibn Ali gives this gloss; al-Alusi also lists obligations as a possible sense and says the comparative allows two analyses."}, {"id": "39:55/q02/p12", "position": "Follow firm obligations and prohibitions.", "reasons": "Al-Tabataba'i reports this narrower view separately from a view including recommended and disliked acts."}, {"id": "39:55/q02/p13", "position": "Follow Quranic guidance to the good of this life and the next, excluding stories and similar material.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi says the comparative is literal on this reading."}, {"id": "39:55/q02/p14", "position": "Practice the better moral teachings, especially pardon, forgiveness, patience, and generous response to wrongs.", "reasons": "Al-Qurtubi reports pardon. Bursevi reports pardon, forgiveness and patience, saying what is best depends on the actor. Al-Biqa'i specifies reconnecting with one who severs ties, giving to one who withholds, and doing good to one who wrongs you."}, {"id": "39:55/q02/p15", "position": "Follow what God taught the Prophet outside the Qur'an, with Qur'anic revelation as the best.", "reasons": "Al-Qurtubi reports this as one explanation, alongside other interpretations."}, {"id": "39:55/q02/p16", "position": "The best is the accounts of earlier peoples.", "reasons": "Al-Qurtubi reports this among other explanations."}, {"id": "39:55/q02/p17", "position": "Follow revelation that shows how to fulfill servanthood through inward belief and action.", "reasons": "Al-Tabataba'i names remembrance, love, true piety and sincere religion; these revive life, faith, deeds and divine guardianship. He says prior submission already encompasses the narrower legal views, making them repetitive without cause. The Najmiyya interpretation cited by Bursevi describes revealed good as what calls people to God, citing 33:46."}, {"id": "39:55/q02/p18", "position": "In worship the highest course is to act as though seeing God.", "reasons": "Al-Biqa'i ranks this above merely remembering that God sees the worshipper."}]}
{"id": "39:55/q03", "question": "Does 'best' rank parts of the Qur'an, and how does its comparative form work?", "turns_on": "Whether God's speech admits intrinsic differences in excellence, whether virtue reports concern content or reward, and whether the comparative here compares Qur'anic parts or expresses complete goodness.", "positions": [{"id": "39:55/q03/p1", "position": "It does not rank Qur'anic parts; all are good, and 'best' can mean complete goodness.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari says the Qur'an's commands, prohibitions, reports, parables, stories, arguments, promises and warnings are all good. Ibn Atiyya relates goodness to human conduct and its consequences. Al-Ash'ari and others, reported by Bursevi, reject intrinsic ranking because all is God's speech and ranking implies inferiority. Ibn Ashur calls ahsan a superlative of complete goodness and compares Joseph preferring prison in 12:33. Kuran Yolu follows him and rejects a translation implying some passages are better. Study Quran and Abu Hayyan compare 39:18."}, {"id": "39:55/q03/p2", "position": "Passages about God's essence, unity and attributes are intrinsically better than passages about other subjects.", "reasons": "Bursevi's preferred view of the verifying scholars ranks al-Ikhlas above al-Masad because the former describes God, whereas the latter's merit is simply being God's speech. Bursevi cites abundant reports of particular chapters' virtues; al-Ghazali's Jawhar al-Qur'an cites Prophetic praise of Yasin, al-Fatiha, the Throne Verse and al-Ikhlas."}, {"id": "39:55/q03/p3", "position": "Differences in a passage's reported excellence can concern its reward while God's eternal speech remains equal in merit.", "reasons": "Bursevi offers this reconciliation for those reluctant to rank verses, including Prophetic expressions such as 'best surah.'"}, {"id": "39:55/q03/p4", "position": "An abrogated ruling can be good even when acting on its replacement is better.", "reasons": "Ali ibn Isa uses this to reject an interpretation that treats 'best' simply as abrogating rather than abrogated revelation."}]}
{"id": "39:55/q04", "question": "How is 'best of what was sent down' constructed grammatically?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "39:55/q04/p1", "position": "'Best' is an adjective annexed to the noun it describes.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur identifies the annexation of ahsan to ma unzila as this construction."}]}
{"id": "39:55/q05", "question": "Which other passages illuminate following the best revelation?", "turns_on": "Which cited scriptural parallel supplies the explanatory context.", "positions": [{"id": "39:55/q05/p1", "position": "It parallels those who listen and follow the best in 39:18.", "reasons": "Al-Nasafi explicitly draws this parallel; Abu Hayyan and Study Quran also mention 39:18 while discussing the scope of 'best.'"}, {"id": "39:55/q05/p2", "position": "It is explained by the instruction in 7:145 to take the best of the revealed material.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzi invokes that verse's matching wording."}]}
{"id": "39:55/q06", "question": "Why say that revelation comes 'from your Lord'?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "39:55/q06/p1", "position": "Naming the Lord encourages obedience by recalling the Benefactor.", "reasons": "Al-Biqa'i says the explicit repeated name encourages even those continuing in grave wrongs; al-Alusi says mentioning the Lord urges obedience to what He sent down."}]}
{"id": "39:55/q07", "question": "Why repeat 'before the punishment comes' with its preposition?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "39:55/q07/p1", "position": "The repetition and retained preposition express God's gentleness to defenseless people.", "reasons": "Al-Biqa'i explains the repeated warning and preposition in these terms."}]}
